```{r, include = FALSE}
online <- requireNamespace("sf", quietly = TRUE) && requireNamespace("jsonlite", quietly = TRUE) &&
  !is.null(tryCatch(curlGetHeaders("https://services1.arcgis.com"), error = function(e) NULL))
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 6, fig.height = 6.5, dev = "ragg_png", dpi = 110, eval = online)
```

```{r, eval = TRUE}
library(phwstyle)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
```

All data on this page is made up. The boundaries are real, and they download
the first time you use a level.

## Draw a map with `phw_map()`

`phw_map()` joins your data to Welsh boundaries and draws a styled map in one
call. Give it your data, the column of area codes (`by`), the column to colour
by (`fill`) and the boundary level. Areas with no row in your data are grey.
The boundary attribution becomes the caption unless you set your own with
`labs()`.

```{r}
codes <- phw_boundaries("health_board")
hb <- tibble(code = codes$code, rate = round(runif(nrow(codes), 20, 80), 1))
```

### Continuous fills

A numeric `fill` gets a continuous scale in the `"blues"` palette. Change it
with `palette`.

```{r, fig.alt = "A map of the health boards of Wales, shaded from light to dark blue by a made-up rate."}
phw_map(hb, by = code, fill = rate, level = "health_board") +
  labs(fill = "Rate per\n100,000", title = "Rate by health board")
```

### Binned fills

Give `bins` a set of breaks, or a single number of bins, to colour by band.
The legend also shows the lowest and highest values, rounded out to tidy
numbers, so both ends of your data are covered.

```{r, fig.alt = "The same health board map with the rate in four bands, and a legend whose first and last bands run from the lowest to the highest value."}
phw_map(hb, by = code, fill = rate, level = "health_board", bins = c(40, 50, 60, 70)) +
  labs(fill = "Rate per\n100,000", title = "Rate by health board")
```

### Groups, with a colour key

A text or factor column gives one colour per group. Give `key` the name of a
colour key and each group keeps its colour in every map, chart and table that
uses it. See [colour keys](colours.html#colours-that-stay-with-their-groups).

```{r, fig.alt = "A map of the health boards of Wales with each board coloured by one of three made-up groups."}
hb$band <- rep_len(c("Group A", "Group B", "Group C"), nrow(hb))
phw_map(hb, by = code, fill = band, level = "health_board", key = "map_groups") +
  labs(fill = NULL, title = "Health boards by group")
```

### Labels

`label` prints text on each area. Give it a column, or an expression built
from the columns of your data and the boundary `name`. When ggrepel is
installed, labels on small areas are moved apart so they stay readable.

```{r, fig.alt = "A map of the local authorities of Wales shaded by a made-up rate, with each area labelled by its name and rate."}
la_codes <- phw_boundaries("local_authority")
la <- tibble(code = la_codes$code, rate = round(runif(nrow(la_codes), 20, 80), 1))
phw_map(la, by = code, fill = rate, level = "local_authority",
        label = paste(name, rate), bins = c(40, 50, 60, 70)) +
  labs(fill = "Rate", title = "Rate by local authority")
```

### One map per period

`phw_map()` takes one row per area and period. Add `facet_wrap()` to draw one
map for each period, on the same scale.

```{r, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.5, fig.alt = "Two maps of the health boards of Wales side by side, one for 2024 and one for 2025, shaded on the same blue scale by a made-up rate."}
hb_years <- tidyr::expand_grid(code = codes$code, year = c(2024, 2025)) |>
  mutate(rate = round(runif(n(), 20, 80), 1))
phw_map(hb_years, by = code, fill = rate, level = "health_board", bins = c(40, 50, 60, 70)) +
  facet_wrap(vars(year)) +
  labs(fill = "Rate", title = "Rate by health board")
```

### Level of detail

`detail` sets how finely the outlines are drawn. The default `"generalised"`
suits most maps. `"super"` and `"ultra"` give smaller files, and `"full"` is
clipped to the coastline.

```{r, fig.alt = "A map of the local authorities of Wales drawn with ultra detail, so the outlines are smooth and simple."}
phw_map(la, by = code, fill = rate, level = "local_authority", detail = "ultra") +
  labs(fill = "Rate", title = "ultra")
```

```{r, fig.alt = "The same local authority map with full detail, so the outlines follow the coastline closely."}
phw_map(la, by = code, fill = rate, level = "local_authority", detail = "full") +
  labs(fill = "Rate", title = "full")
```

## Build your own map

`phw_boundaries()` returns an `sf` data frame with `code`, `name`, `name_cy`
(where the source has Welsh names) and the geometry. Join your own data on
`code`, then draw it with `geom_sf()`. `scale_fill_phw_b()` gives a binned
scale and `theme_phw_map()` removes the axes and grid.

```{r, fig.alt = "A map of the health boards of Wales shaded in blue bands by a made-up rate, drawn with geom_sf."}
hb_sf <- phw_boundaries("health_board") |>
  left_join(hb, by = "code")

ggplot(hb_sf) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = rate), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_phw_b(name = "Rate per\n100,000") +
  theme_phw_map() +
  labs(title = "Rate by health board",
       caption = paste(strwrap(attr(hb_sf, "attribution"), 60), collapse = "\n"))
```

## Levels

`phw_boundary_levels()` lists every level and the release used for it. GP
clusters, LSOAs and the other levels work like the examples above.

```{r, eval = TRUE}
phw_boundary_levels()
```

```{r, fig.alt = "A map of the GP clusters of Wales in one light teal colour."}
gp <- phw_boundaries("gp_cluster")
ggplot(gp) +
  geom_sf(fill = phw_colours[["light_teal"]], colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  theme_phw_map() +
  labs(title = paste(nrow(gp), "GP clusters"))
```

## Interactive maps

`phw_leaflet()` starts a leaflet map on Wales, with a light grey base map.
`phw_leaflet_polygons()` adds your areas. It takes the same `fill`, `bins` and
`key` as `phw_map()`, plus `label` and `popup` for what appears on hover and
click. Ask for longitude and latitude with `crs = 4326`.

```{r, eval = online && requireNamespace("leaflet", quietly = TRUE)}
hb_ll <- phw_boundaries("health_board", crs = 4326) |>
  left_join(hb, by = "code")
phw_leaflet() |>
  phw_leaflet_polygons(hb_ll, fill = rate, bins = 4, label = name, legend_title = "Rate")
```

`phw_leaflet_palette()` makes the colour function that
`phw_leaflet_polygons()` uses. Use it when you add layers with leaflet itself
and want the same colours.

```{r, eval = online && requireNamespace("leaflet", quietly = TRUE)}
pal <- phw_leaflet_palette("blues", domain = hb_ll$rate, type = "bin", bins = 4)
phw_leaflet() |>
  leaflet::addPolygons(data = hb_ll, fillColor = ~pal(rate), fillOpacity = 0.8,
                       weight = 1, color = "#FFFFFF", label = ~name) |>
  leaflet::addLegend(pal = pal, values = hb_ll$rate, title = "Rate")
```

For more interactive output, see [the interactive article](interactive.html).
For finished examples, see the [gallery](gallery.html#maps).

## Keeping boundaries up to date

When ONS or the Welsh Government publish new boundaries, a new version of
phwstyle points to them. After updating phwstyle, refresh your cached
copies:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
phw_boundaries("electoral_ward", refresh = TRUE)
phw_boundaries_cache(clear = TRUE)   # or clear everything
```

You don't have to update phwstyle for your maps to keep working:

- Boundaries you have already downloaded are read from your cache, so they
  don't change and don't need a connection.
- Where a geography has two sources, the second is used if the first can't
  be reached.
- If a publisher withdraws a layer that your version of phwstyle lists,
  `phw_boundaries()` fetches the current list of layers from the phwstyle
  repository on GitHub and uses that. The list is checked against both
  publishers every week. Set `options(phwstyle.boundary_update = FALSE)` if
  you'd rather it didn't look.
- If nothing can be downloaded, boundaries saved from an earlier release are
  returned with a warning.

In each of those cases a warning says what you were given.
